heritage.name: Gaelic Irish of Leinster
heritage.homeland: County Wexford and neighbouring southeastern Ireland
heritage.migrationStory: People from southeastern Ireland moved to Britain and North America, especially during the 19th century. Wexford emigrants also joined Irish communities in Australia.
heritage.funFact: Wexford is one of Murphy’s strongest historic heartlands.

research.meaning: Murphy means “descendant of Murchadh,” an Irish personal name combining muir, “sea,” and cath, “battle.” Murchadh is commonly interpreted as “sea warrior”; the surname itself does not prove a seafaring ancestry.
research.summary: Murphy is Ireland’s most common surname, with particularly strong historical roots in County Wexford and County Cork. Several distinct Irish families adopted the name independently, and centuries of migration carried it to Britain, North America, Australia and beyond.
research.originStory: In medieval Ireland, families began using Ó Murchadha, meaning “descendant of Murchadh,” to identify descent from an ancestor bearing that personal name. Because Murchadh was used by different families, there was no single founder of all Murphys. Important Murphy lineages developed in Leinster and Munster, especially in present-day Wexford and Cork.

timeline.event: As hereditary surnames spread in Ireland, different families formed names meaning “descendant of Murchadh.”
Murphy families became established in Leinster and Munster, with enduring concentrations in Wexford and Cork.
English-language administration increasingly recorded Irish surnames in anglicised forms; Murphy often appeared without the Ó prefix.
The Great Famine and continuing economic hardship accelerated Irish migration to Britain, North America and Australia.
Census and modern surname statistics document Murphy as Ireland’s most common surname, also widespread throughout the Irish diaspora.

heritageOptions.funFact: Cork’s famous Murphy’s stout was founded by members of the Murphy family in 1856.

heritageOptions.homeland: Ulster, including Counties Armagh and Tyrone
heritageOptions.migrationStory: Murphy families from Ulster joined migrations to Scotland, England and North America during the 18th and 19th centuries. Their descendants became part of both Irish and wider Ulster emigrant communities.
heritageOptions.funFact: Murphy is found across Ireland’s provinces, not just in its southern heartlands.

funFacts: Murphy is Ireland’s most common surname.
The Ó in its Irish forms means “descendant of,” rather than simply “son of.”
The personal name behind Murphy contains the Irish word for “sea.”
Ó Murchadha and Ó Murchú are related Irish forms of the surname.
Two Murphy families can share a surname without sharing a recent ancestor.
research.caveat: Murphy strongly suggests Irish surname origins, but spelling alone cannot identify a county, clan, religion or ethnicity. The regional options are historical possibilities, not personal ancestry estimates; records of your earliest known ancestors are needed to distinguish them.

outline.title: The Sea Between Two Halves
outline.tagline: A broken weaving shuttle carries Aoife across an ocean—and into her family's unfinished promise.
outline.logline: Fourteen-year-old Aoife Murphy discovers half a wooden weaving shuttle in a Boston family trunk and is swept into her ancestors’ County Wexford home. Following its missing half through famine, migration, and another generation’s crisis, she discovers that keeping a family together sometimes means helping it live apart.

heirloom.name: The Split Shuttle
heirloom.description: Half of a polished wooden weaving shuttle, with a brass tip, a carved wave, and the letters Ó Murchadha scratched along its edge. Its matching half bears the rest of the wave; when Aoife touches the broken edge, it carries her to moments when her family’s future changed, but only joining the halves will open her way home.

outline.mystery: Who kept the other half of the shuttle?

cast.name: Eileen Murphy
cast.role: Aoife’s ancestor; a young Wexford weaver who emigrates to Boston
cast.look: Nineteen in 1844, short and sturdy, with a round freckled face, dark auburn hair braided around her head, and a blue wool shawl over a patched brown dress; later appearances retain the shawl and show her aging.

cast.name: Tomás Murphy
cast.role: Eileen’s younger brother, who remains in Wexford
cast.look: Fourteen in 1844, lanky, with a narrow face, straight black hair, and a conspicuous gap between his front teeth; wears a rust-colored neckerchief and an oversized gray jacket, with age-appropriate changes in later appearances.

cast.name: Mr. Keane
cast.role: A fictional estate agent whose rent demands threaten the family home
cast.look: Forty-five, tall and angular, with sandy side-whiskers, thin lips, a dark fitted coat, and a leather rent ledger tucked beneath one arm.

cast.name: Nora Murphy
cast.role: Tomás’s granddaughter; a later emigrant and Boston nurse
cast.look: Twenty-four in 1918, broad-shouldered, with brown skin weathered by outdoor work, dark eyes, and black hair pinned into a tight bun; wears a white nursing apron and carries a small green traveling case.

acts.title: A Wave in the Wood
acts.beat: Aoife, fourteen, with wild red curls, freckles, and a green raincoat, finds the broken shuttle beneath family letters in a trunk, alongside a photograph labeled 'Wexford.' When she traces its carved wave, her kitchen dissolves into a weaving room, and she discovers that the shuttle will not take her home while its other half is missing.
acts.history: Boston became a major home for Irish immigrants and their descendants, but a shared surname alone cannot establish a particular family’s ancestry.

acts.title: The Name at the Loom
acts.place: A fictional family household near Enniscorthy, County Wexford
acts.beat: Eileen welcomes the bewildered Aoife into a household supported by weaving, seasonal labor, and a small potato plot, while Tomás teaches her to wind yarn without tangling it. When Mr. Keane arrives with a rent demand, Aoife notices that his ledger calls them 'Murphy' although their father carved 'Ó Murchadha' on the shuttle, and Eileen explains that neither spelling can pay their arrears.
acts.history: Ó Murchadha means 'descendant of Murchadh,' a personal name containing words for 'sea' and 'battle'; hereditary Irish surnames developed across different families, and English-language records often used anglicized forms.

acts.title: The Empty Ridge
acts.beat: Repeated potato failures destroy the household’s food supply, and Aoife helps Eileen seek relief while rent arrears grow and Mr. Keane threatens eviction. A relative in Boston sends passage money for one person; Eileen and Tomás divide their late father’s shuttle as a promise to meet again, but the heirloom pulls Aoife onward before she sees where Tomás puts his half.
acts.history: The Great Famine of 1845–1852 combined potato blight with poverty, unequal access to resources, and inadequate relief, causing mass death and migration while many families remained in Ireland.

acts.title: Beyond the Irish Sea
acts.place: Wexford to Liverpool, then Halifax and Boston
acts.beat: Aoife follows Eileen by coastal passage to Liverpool, where confusing tickets, lodging costs, and the fear of losing her remaining money make departure nearly fail. A prepaid berth aboard Cunard’s Britannia secures the Atlantic crossing through Halifax to Boston, but a violent storm forces Eileen to choose between protecting her bundle and helping a frightened fellow passenger.
acts.history: Liverpool was a major departure port for Irish emigrants, and Cunard’s Britannia served the Liverpool–Halifax–Boston route; passage conditions differed greatly between vessels and ticket classes.

acts.title: A Room of Their Own
acts.beat: Eileen finds crowded lodgings and domestic work, but low wages, anti-Irish prejudice, and an employer who delays payment threaten her ability to send money home. With help from neighbors she secures better work and begins sending remittances to Tomás, whose letters reveal that staying in Wexford is a choice shaped by obligations—not a failure to be brave.
acts.history: Famine-era Irish immigrants in Boston often faced overcrowding, insecure employment, and nativist hostility, while remittances helped relatives survive and financed later migration.

acts.title: The Green Traveling Case
acts.place: Boston, with letters and memories from County Wexford
acts.beat: The shuttle carries Aoife into an influenza-stricken Boston, where an elderly Eileen waits for Nora, Tomás’s granddaughter, who emigrated before the war and now tends sick households. Nora’s green case is mislaid during an emergency transfer; Aoife helps recover it and finds Tomás’s half inside, wrapped in his letter asking Nora to complete the reunion he never managed.
acts.history: Boston suffered severely during the 1918 influenza pandemic, and Irish migration continued across generations as family networks connected new arrivals with established communities.

acts.title: The Whole Wave
acts.beat: Nora gives Eileen the missing half, revealing that Tomás kept it throughout his life before entrusting it to his granddaughter, and Aoife helps their trembling hands fit the carved wave together. The completed shuttle opens her way home, where she finds it whole in the family trunk and begins recording the letters’ names and dates, determined to preserve both the relatives who left and those who stayed.
acts.history: Family letters, heirlooms, civil records, and census returns can help reconstruct a specific migration story, whereas surname meanings cannot prove an individual family’s route.

historyNote.title: Did you know? Letters can lead home
historyNote.body: Boston became a major home for Irish immigrants and their descendants, especially during and after the Great Famine of 1845–1852. art.locations: All panels take place in the same modest Murphy family weaving room near Enniscorthy, County Wexford, in 1844. The small room has rough whitewashed stone walls, a low exposed-beam ceiling, an earthen floor, and one narrow window admitting cool, soft daylight. A large, weathered wooden handloom dominates the room, with yarn hanging from pegs beside it and a few simple baskets of wool kept unobtrusively near the wall. The whole wooden shuttle rests on the loom; its brass tip, carved wave, and scratched family name match the broken half Aoife holds. The atmosphere is quiet and intimate, with muted browns, stone creams, and wool blues; magical light, when present, is a restrained pale gold rising from the carved wave.

art.locations: One continuous location: the Murphy family weaving room near Enniscorthy, County Wexford, in 1844. A small, plain stone cottage room with a low timber ceiling, rough plastered walls, packed-earth floor, and a wooden handloom occupying the rear wall; undyed yarn hangs beside it. A worn worktable and a small wooden bobbin sit in the foreground. The open doorway is on the right wall, with a modest potato plot visible outside in soft daylight. Cool, overcast daylight enters through the doorway and a small window, muted earth browns and gray stone contrasted with the blue shawl and yarn. Keep the loom, yarn, table, doorway, plot, and light consistent in every panel.

historyNote.title: Did you know? One name, different forms
historyNote.body: Murphy is an English-language form of the Irish surname Ó Murchadha, meaning “descendant of Murchadh.” The personal name Murchadh contains Irish words for “sea” and “battle.” English-language records often used forms such as Murphy without the Ó prefix. Different Irish families developed this surname, so there was no single ancestor of every Murphy.

dialectWord.meaning: Descendant of; used at the beginning of many Irish surnames.

quiz.question: Why does the ledger say Murphy while the shuttle says Ó Murchadha?

quiz.explanation: English-language records often used Murphy where an Irish name appeared as Ó Murchadha.
